# ApexToWWW

> Free DNS service that 301-redirects apex/naked domains to their www subdomain. Two DNS records, automatic SSL via Let's Encrypt, IPv6 and HTTP/3 support, no signup required.

## Quick facts

- **What it does**: HTTP 301 redirect from `example.com` to `www.example.com`
- **Setup**: Point apex A record to `65.21.184.101` and AAAA to `2a01:4f9:c012:a304::1`
- **Cost**: Free, no premium tier, no usage limits, no account required
- **SSL**: Automatic Let's Encrypt certificates, provisioned on first request
- **Protocols**: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 (QUIC)
- **IP stack**: IPv4 + IPv6 dual-stack
- **Redirect latency**: Under 50ms
- **Path preservation**: Full path + query string preserved (301 redirect is RFC 7231 compliant)
- **Infrastructure**: ARM64 servers (Hetzner), energy-efficient
- **Provider**: Sandbox.ventures, based in Aarhus, Denmark
- **Contact**: hi@apextowww.com

## The problem ApexToWWW solves

Apex domains (also called root, naked, or bare domains — the domain without any prefix, e.g. `example.com` rather than `www.example.com`) cannot use CNAME records. This is mandated by [RFC 1034 §3.6.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034#section-3.6.2) and [RFC 2181 §10.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2181#section-10.1), which forbid CNAME records at the zone apex because they conflict with the required SOA and NS records.

Most modern hosting platforms (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, Heroku, Firebase Hosting, Cloudflare Pages) require a CNAME for custom domains. This creates an incompatibility: users expect `example.com` to work, but DNS doesn't allow it to CNAME to the hosting provider.

Common workarounds include:
- **ALIAS / ANAME records** — not universally supported, often paid DNS
- **CNAME flattening** — requires moving nameservers to Cloudflare
- **Provider-specific A records** — can break when the provider changes IPs
- **A/AAAA redirect to www** — what ApexToWWW does, permanently and for free

## How it works

1. User types `example.com` in a browser
2. DNS resolves apex to `65.21.184.101` (or IPv6 equivalent)
3. ApexToWWW server receives the request and detects the Host header
4. Server responds with `HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently` and `Location: https://www.example.com[original path]`
5. Browser follows redirect to www subdomain, which points to the user's actual hosting

The SSL certificate for the apex domain is provisioned automatically via Let's Encrypt using the HTTP-01 challenge on first request.

## Setup guide

```
A     @     65.21.184.101
AAAA  @     2a01:4f9:c012:a304::1
```

That's it. No signup, no dashboard, no API keys.

DNS propagation typically takes 5-30 minutes. SSL is provisioned on first HTTPS request to the apex.

## Verification

```
curl -I https://example.com
```

Expected response:
```
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://www.example.com/
```

## Limitations

- **Wildcard domains are not supported** — we verify DNS ownership before issuing certificates
- Your www subdomain must be configured separately (CNAME to your hosting provider)
- Not suitable if you want apex to serve content directly (use ALIAS records instead)

## Works with

- GitHub Pages
- Netlify
- Vercel
- Heroku
- Firebase Hosting
- Cloudflare Pages
- AWS CloudFront
- AWS Amplify Hosting
- Render
- Fly.io
- Any hosting platform requiring www CNAME

## Standards and references

- [RFC 1034 — Domain names: concepts and facilities](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034) — defines the zone apex and CNAME exclusivity rule
- [RFC 2181 — Clarifications to the DNS Specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2181#section-10.1) — clarifies SOA/NS/CNAME interaction at zone apex
- [RFC 7231 §6.4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-6.4.2) — 301 Moved Permanently semantics
- [Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/) — certificate authority used for automatic SSL
